For many, the underworld’s stranglehold on Bollywood through the 1990s is still a raw memory. The attack on Shroff, whose father, Jackie, is a loved figure in the film industry, comes on the back of threats to several other stars. Those who have been threatened in the last two years include Salman Khan, his brother-in-law, actor Ayush Sharma, director Rohit Shetty, and Ranveer Singh. Politician Baba Siddiqui, killed in October 2024, was a close friend of Bollywood A-listers including Salman Khan and Shah Rukh Khan. In the same month as Siddique’s killing, stand-up comic Munawar Faruqui was provided police cover after threats from the Bishnoi gang. In July this year, actor Aamir Khan was warned about indulging in ‘Love Jihad’ by the same gang following his wedding to Gauri Spratt. Deep Dive But what has rattled the Mumbai film industry is the audacity of the attack on Shroff from such close range. Three motorbike-borne men fired seven rounds from a sophisticated semi-automatic Zigana handgun at his car in Juhu at 7pm amid Navratri season when the area was choc-a-bloc with traffic. The attackers were unmasked and unconcerned about being caught. “They were also watching him. How else did they know that he routinely went to the Pushpa Narsee Park to play football every Sunday?” said a leading man who often plays football with Tiger Shroff at the same venue. In Mumbai, top stars have resorted to private security. “The attack on Tiger has taken us back to the 90s. I am just going to add a few more people to my retinue of bodyguards,” said a famous action star of the 1990s. “This attack has left me really frightened. I have three guards. But are they enough?” He added that if he, too, like his friends Salman Khan and Shetty, has to disappear behind a wall of security. Salman Khan has a Y Plus security in addition to a private detail. In June 2022, a note was left on the promenade at Bandra Bandstand for the actor’s screenwriter father, Salim Khan, at his usual bench, warning that his son could meet the same fate as singer Sidhu Moosewala, who was assassinated in Punjab in 2022. The last two years have been traumatic for Salman Khan, who has drastically cut down on his public appearances. Shetty’s life has been circumscribed since shots were fired at his house in Juhu in February this year. His set for ‘Golmaal-5’, helmed by Ajay Devgn, was as secure as Fort Knox (a major US Army installation in Kentucky), said an actor who worked on the film. “We created a bubble around Rohit. There were no outsiders allowed, and other than the actors and the senior technical team, no one was allowed close to him. His security was iron-clad,” said a wardrobe assistant who worked on the film, describing the atmosphere on set as “extremely stressful.” A film producer said the industry had only a few years ago begun to emerge from the shadows of the 1990s when the writ of the Mumbai mafia ran unchecked. “Extortions, forcible casting, shootouts, killings…that had all stopped in the last few years, and we thought the worst was behind us. But it seems to be changing. My antenna went up when I heard that they [Bishnoi gang members] asked Ranveer Singh to pay extortion money after the success of ‘Dhurandhar’. That kind of thing makes us all vulnerable. Our high profile makes us soft targets, and we have little assurance from the administration or the police.” People aware of the matter said that Mumbai Police have not received any complaints of extortion from anyone in the film industry so far.

news.headline: AISA president Neha Bora moves Delhi HC, challenges police notice to execute bond
news.story_lead: AISA president Neha Bora moves Delhi HC, challenges police notice to execute bond In her petition, Neha Bora said the SEM’s notice was prima facie ambiguous, factually incorrect and violates Articles 19 and 21 of the Constitution. All India Students’ Association (AISA) president Neha Bora on Monday moved the Delhi high court, challenging a police notice directing her to furnish a personal bond of ₹ 10,000, along with one surety, to “maintain peace during the period of inquiry” following her participation in a flag march. A New Delhi district police officer, designated as the Special Executive Magistrate (SEM), directed her to appear before it on Monday and execute a bond.
news.full_article_text: AISA president Neha Bora moves Delhi HC, challenges police notice to execute bond In her petition, Neha Bora said the SEM’s notice was prima facie ambiguous, factually incorrect and violates Articles 19 and 21 of the Constitution. All India Students’ Association (AISA) president Neha Bora on Monday moved the Delhi high court, challenging a police notice directing her to furnish a personal bond of ₹ 10,000, along with one surety, to “maintain peace during the period of inquiry” following her participation in a flag march. A New Delhi district police officer, designated as the Special Executive Magistrate (SEM), directed her to appear before it on Monday and execute a bond. The order was issued on October 17 (Saturday), the same day she was released after being detained on Friday for participating in the flag march. Also Read | AISA's Neha Bora released, CJP's Abhijeet Dipke arrested; police to file 7-8 FIRs amid anti-EC stir Bora challenges ₹ 10,000 bond notice in Delhi HC The notice cited three grounds for requiring her to execute the bond: alleged sloganeering at Mandi House on October 16; repeated protests in the vicinity of Jantar Mantar despite prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS); and the allegation that, on October 16, she instigated people to participate in a protest at Connaught Place. In her petition filed through advocate Abhik Chimni, Bora said the notice was prima facie ambiguous, factually incorrect and violates Articles 19 and 21 of the Constitution. The notice does not produce any material or information to substantiate the “likelihood” of breach of peace, fails to disclose the period, occasion or event in relation to which a breach is apprehended, the petition said. Also Read | Abhijeet Dipke, Neha Bora among 150 detained in Delhi; Oppn slams police action amid anti-CEC protests Petition disputes allegation of instigating protest While the high court remains on vacation until October 25, Bora’s legal team said that it would press the petition, which challenges the allegation on the ground that it rests on a prima facie incorrect factual premise—namely, that she instigated people to participate in the demonstration at Central Park, Connaught Place, on October 16, 2026, for an urgent hearing this week. The petition said that her call and the incident in question were distinct, asserting that she called for a peaceful gathering at Mandi House at 5pm on the same day. It further pointed out that she was detained at Mandi House. Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) convenor Abhijeet Dipke, announced a flag march on Friday evening after his party’s co-convenors, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were arrested for unfurling the national flag at Jantar Mantar last Tuesday. The duo were sent to five days’ judicial custody. Bora, who started her flag march with AISA activists at Mandi House at 5.15 pm, was detained from there. Bora, who was released on Saturday at 6am after being held for 12 hours, had also criticised the police action. "The current movement has clearly exposed how people are being detained, whether during the day or in the evening, held in custody throughout the night, and only released the following morning or evening. Under what authority is this justified? By what law or order is it permissible to keep detainees held in custody all night long? Legally, individuals, especially women, ought to be released after sunset, yet this is not happening.”

news.headline: Keeping up with UP: Can Rahul Gandhi’s street activism revive the Congress in UP?
news.story_lead: Keeping up with UP: Can Rahul Gandhi’s street activism revive the Congress in UP? Can the Congress or its cadre in Uttar Pradesh amplify Rahul Gandhi's combative mood or remain bogged down with internecine troubles? On the day Congress leader Rahul Gandhi was protesting in the streets of Delhi, belligerently raising the public issue of ‘vote chori’, Congressmen in Lucknow publicly exchanged blows, seemingly over organisational changes, at the party headquarters.
news.full_article_text: Keeping up with UP: Can Rahul Gandhi’s street activism revive the Congress in UP? Can the Congress or its cadre in Uttar Pradesh amplify Rahul Gandhi's combative mood or remain bogged down with internecine troubles? On the day Congress leader Rahul Gandhi was protesting in the streets of Delhi, belligerently raising the public issue of ‘vote chori’, Congressmen in Lucknow publicly exchanged blows, seemingly over organisational changes, at the party headquarters. That their leader was being battered and bruised did not worry them. Nor did the fact that the crucial assembly elections are coming up and the party’s prospects remained seemingly dismal. Watching with dismay were senior Congress leaders, including the party deputy leader in the Rajya Sabha, Pramod Tiwari, and his MLA daughter, Aradhana Mishra, the newly elected Uttar Pradesh Congress Committee (UPCC) president. It was her first day in office. Significantly, the scuffle involved the outgoing firebrand president Ajay Rai and a lesser-known woman corporator. The ugly scenes in the party office literally threw cold water on the hard work of their leader, whose various street strategies have evoked hopes but have yet to generate votes – remember, Congress has lost Bihar and UP looks distant. The reasons are many, including the image of a naïve politician the BJP has built of Rahul Gandhi Gandhi’s public image has perceptibly improved, even though Modi supporters lose no opportunity to ridicule him for his political naivety. The old narrative that started from the times of the country's first prime minister, ‘After Nehru, who?’ or the perennial TINA (There Is No Alternative), remains in the air in favour of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. But can the Congress or its cadre in Uttar Pradesh amplify his combative mood or remain bogged down with internecine troubles? Infighting is not new to Congress; rather, it persists in every political party from top to bottom. Congress' history of infighting Old Congressmen recall the days of Kamlapati Tripathi vs Chandra Bhanu Gupta who despite their internal rivalry often cooperated strategically to engineer the downfall of their common rival like Sampurnanand. Later, the party infighting took a caste hue with the emergence of Rajput leadership in the 1980s and for several decades, it remained infested with a Brahmin vs Rajput one-upmanship war. Sanjay Singh, the titular Raja of Amethi, was tipped to be the chief minister in 1980, but after much celebration, he was dropped in favour of another Rajput Vishwanath Pratap Singh, who went on to become India’s seventh prime minister. Singh launched both the Bofors campaign against Rajiv Gandhi and the Mandal initiative, granting quotas for the OBCs. Congress leaders fought with each other -- Kamlapati Tripathi’s family from Varanasi vs Vir Bahadur Singh from Gorakhpur, ND Tiwari vs Vir Bahadur Singh, et al. Even Sripati Mishra, who replaced Vishwanath Pratap Singh in 1982, faced furious dissidence during his three-year tenure. While they were stalwarts who were remote-controlled by Delhi, here a corporator was taking on an outgoing state chief of the party, Ajay Rai, who, irrespective of his temperament, had travelled the state extensively to galvanise the party. He not only gave a spirited fight against the country's PM in the Varanasi Lok Sabha constituency in 2024, but the party's overall tally also improved under his leadership. The organisational changes in the Congress, made on the eve of elections, were also apparently triggered by the infighting that continues to plague the party. The former AICC general secretary in charge of UP affairs, Avinash Pandey, and Ajay Rai had teamed up well. But soon after Pandey was replaced by Rajendra Pal Gautam, a prominent Dalit leader, speculation started about Rai's removal. Rai’s family was in Congress, but he had started his political career in the BJP. He wore a vermilion tikka on his forehead and frequently visited temples. Gautam came from AAP via BSP and visited Sarnath during his trip to Varanasi. Political experts believe the Congress high command erred by implementing organisational changes just ahead of the elections. Though Rahul Gandhi spoke to Rai before the announcement, Rai perhaps felt humiliated. Undoubtedly, he is a strongman with muscle and money power, but he kept waiting for Delhi to appoint his organisational team. The soft-spoken, newly appointed chief, Mishra, also needs time to win the party's confidence and galvanise it for the polls. Though her father, Pramod Tiwari, can fix nuts and bolts with his long experience as a nine-time MLA, the time is too short to prepare the party to face a tough battle against the BJP by ensuring basic bonhomie among the cadres of the allies. Paradoxically, while the state unit needs to replicate its leader's street activism in Lucknow on local and hyperlocal issues, they are engaging in physical altercations, knowing fully well that an opportunity lies ahead to ride their strong poll partner - the Samajwadi Party. The BJP too is a divided house, and there is anti-incumbency against the 10-year Yogi government, even though CM's personal image has so far remained untarnished. Gandhi has built an image of a combative leader, but his party here remains in limbo, though sporadic protests have been simultaneously organised in the state. But for a more aggressive approach, the party will have to navigate internal contradictions, besides coordinating with the Samajwadi Party. As of now, people are comparing Rahul’s aggressive street performance -- including demonstrations, climbing barricades, and facing cops -- with his grandmother Indira Gandhi’s fight against the Janata Party, which had catapulted her to power within three years. “In the run-up to the January 1980 general elections, Indira spent 62 days on the road (and in the air), covering 40,000 miles and addressing up to twenty meetings a day. An estimated 90 million people -- or one in every four of the Indian electorate -- throughout the country saw and heard Indira Gandhi in the course of her last and most arduous campaign,” writes Katherine Frank in her book Indira: The Life of Indira Nehru Gandhi. news.full_article_text: Beyond fighter jets: What India needs to prepare for the wars of tomorrow In a conversation with HT Senior Anchor Aayesha Varma on Point Blank, Executive Editor Shishir Gupta argued that India must look beyond fleet numbers. India’s airpower debate is no longer simply about how many fighter jets the country needs. It is about what those aircraft can achieve in skies increasingly threatened by long-range missiles, drones and sophisticated air defences. In a conversation with Hindustan Times Senior Anchor Aayesha Varma on Point Blank, Executive Editor Shishir Gupta argued that India must look beyond fleet numbers. More fighters remain necessary, but they must form part of a wider military capability combining unmanned systems, longer-range weapons and layered defences. The central objective is deterrence: preventing an adversary from attacking by making the likely costs unacceptably high. More fighters, but not numbers alone The discussion began with Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh’s call to induct 38–40 fighters annually as the Indian Air Force seeks to rebuild its declining strength. Gupta said the fleet had fallen below 30 squadrons, against a benchmark of approximately 42.5. He also drew a distinction over that benchmark, saying it had been authorised by the Chairman, Chiefs of Staff Committee, rather than the Cabinet Committee on Security. Yet the numerical shortfall tells only part of the story. Gupta questioned whether adding aircraft, without improving the weapons they carry, would deliver sufficient military advantage. His argument centred on standoff weapons: missiles and other munitions that allow aircraft to strike from farther away, reducing their exposure to hostile air defences. A larger fighter fleet becomes more useful when its aircraft can attack without having to fly deep into an adversary’s defensive envelope. Why range changes the equation For Gupta, the priority is not choosing between aircraft and missiles, but ensuring they work together. Longer-range air-to-air weapons can threaten enemy aircraft at greater distances. Air-to-ground weapons can allow pilots to attack targets while remaining farther from defensive systems. The same logic, he argued, should influence where India stations its aircraft, with attention to protecting bases from enemy strikes. He also cautioned against viewing India’s requirements primarily through Pakistan. China, he said, must shape the longer-term assessment of the scale and sophistication of the threat. That shifts the question from “How many fighters are enough?” to something more demanding: what combination of aircraft, weapons and protected infrastructure can remain effective against a powerful adversary? Also Read | Does India need stand-off missiles or more fighter jets? What drone warfare does - and does not - prove Gupta pointed to Ukraine, Iran and the Houthis to illustrate how forces with limited conventional airpower can use missiles and drones to impose costs on stronger opponents. In his assessment, attacks on infrastructure demonstrate that military pressure need not depend entirely on a large fighter fleet. Relatively inexpensive weapons can also create an uncomfortable economic imbalance when defenders use costly interceptors against them. But he stopped short of arguing that India should abandon manned aircraft. India, he said, has too much at stake to rely exclusively on drones, loitering munitions or missiles. The lesson is therefore not that fighters have become irrelevant. It is that they cannot be expected to deliver every military objective by themselves. Gupta’s preferred approach combines manned and unmanned capabilities according to the target, the adversary and the intended outcome. Also Read | ‘Delay in inducting new fighter jets hurting IAF’: Air Chief Marshal AP Singh highlights need for strengthening IAF A shield must match the threat The discussion also highlighted the importance of defending against the weapons transforming offensive warfare. Gupta argued that India needs a layered response rather than a single, all-purpose shield. Different threats require different interception options, particularly when the cost of destroying a cheap drone can far exceed the cost of launching it. He discussed systems ranging from lower-level interception capabilities to Akash and the S-400, alongside indigenous interceptor development. His broader point was that defensive planning must account for both effectiveness and affordability. The stakes extend beyond military installations. Gupta linked protection against missile attacks to civilian morale and economic confidence. In that framing, air and missile defence are not merely supporting capabilities; they help preserve the stability on which national growth depends. Also Read | ‘Definitely no’: Ex-Air Force vice chief questions relevance of Tejas Mk-2 fighter jets in mid 2030s, slams HAL delay Building reach around existing aircraft Gupta identified several weapons programmes as important to strengthening India’s existing and future aircraft. These included work on a lighter BrahMos missile for smaller fighters, the Rudram anti-radiation missile programme and longer-range Astra air-to-air missiles. He presented them as complementary efforts to extend striking power and expand the distances at which India can threaten hostile aircraft or engage targets. The underlying procurement argument is significant: improving the weapons available to a fighter can be as important as acquiring the aircraft itself. He also placed airpower within a wider deterrence framework that includes conventional missiles, submarines and underwater drones. The emphasis was on building multiple military options rather than making one platform responsible for national security. The fifth-generation fighter dilemma That same reasoning shaped Gupta’s assessment of fifth-generation aircraft. He acknowledged the value of advanced fighters and discussed stealth features such as carrying weapons internally to reduce radar visibility. But he rejected the idea that acquiring such aircraft would, by itself, resolve India’s security challenges. With a finite defence budget, expensive fighters must be weighed against other requirements, including unmanned combat systems and missile defence. Gupta’s central prescription was a balanced force: advanced aircraft where they add decisive value, longer-range weapons to improve their effectiveness, unmanned systems to broaden operational choices, and defences that protect the country against retaliation. Relatively inexpensive weapons can also create an uncomfortable economic imbalance when defenders use costly interceptors against them. But he stopped short of arguing that India should abandon manned aircraft. India, he said, has too much at stake to rely exclusively on drones, loitering munitions or missiles. news.headline: On camera, Tiger Shroff shooting suspects seen rushing to catch train in Surat before arrest in Kota
news.story_lead: On camera, Tiger Shroff shooting suspects seen rushing to catch train in Surat before arrest in Kota The three suspects were nabbed on Monday from Rajasthan's Kota from where they were planning to flee to Nepal via Delhi. Fresh details have emerged in the shooting case involving Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff, with CCTV footage from Surat railway station helping police track down the three alleged assailants, who were arrested in Rajasthan’s Kota on Monday. Shroff escaped unhurt after three motorcycle-borne assailants opened fire at him in Mumbai on Sunday evening as he was leaving a club in his car after playing football.
news.full_article_text: On camera, Tiger Shroff shooting suspects seen rushing to catch train in Surat before arrest in Kota The three suspects were nabbed on Monday from Rajasthan's Kota from where they were planning to flee to Nepal via Delhi. Fresh details have emerged in the shooting case involving Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff, with CCTV footage from Surat railway station helping police track down the three alleged assailants, who were arrested in Rajasthan’s Kota on Monday. Shroff escaped unhurt after three motorcycle-borne assailants opened fire at him in Mumbai on Sunday evening as he was leaving a club in his car after playing football. The suspects subsequently travelled by road from Mumbai to Surat, where they boarded the Pune-Jaipur Express (train 12939). They were arrested in Kota on Monday morning while allegedly attempting to flee to Nepal via Delhi . Also read: Shooters planned to kill Tiger Shroff in Mumbai, motive unclear, say police According to railway officials, a team of Railway Police Force (RPF) and Government Railway Police (GRP) was formed based on inputs received from the police. "The surveillance footage was checked at various stations after which they were tracked from Surat railway station. The team of rail police along with local police apprehended them at Kota the next day, at around 10.15 am," said a Western Railway official. Fresh clip shows men rushing to catch train Deep Dive Two CCTV footages seen by HT show the trio rushing their way to catch the train. Two of the three men are dressed in white shirts, while the third one is seen wearing a blue T-shirt, carrying a bag. They can be seen walking hurriedly outside the station. On the platform, the trio is seen rushing past the crowd to catch the train – two running ahead and the third one closely following behind. The CCTV footages became a crucial piece of evidence for the cops who were trying to nab the assailants in the high-profile case. How investigators tracked the assailants The three suspects were detained from the general coach of the Pune-Jaipur Express when the train arrived at Kota railway station. According to the RPF, Kota division received information from the Mumbai Police crime branch about the suspects travelling on the train in connection with the firing incident in Juhu. "The joint team checked the train upon its arrival and detained the three men before they could proceed further. Preliminary information indicated that the suspects had travelled by road from Mumbai to Surat before boarding the train," said the railway official. Who are the assailants? The suspects have been identified as Rehan alias Sukka (18), a resident of Sonipat in Haryana; Ritwik Kurmi alias Roshan Fighter (22), reportedly from Bihar and currently residing in Andheri West. While the third suspect was initially said to be a minor, the cops later clarified that all the three men are adults – the third one identified as 18-years-old-Phool Singh. One of the accused is said to be a driver working for app based aggregator Rapido. A spokesperson for the company said in a statement: "We are deeply concerned by the incident involving Mr. Tiger Shroff and his team, and we are relieved that he is safe. We wish him a swift recovery. We are aware of media reports mentioning an individual registered as a captain on the Rapido platform. He has not been active as a captain on our platform since 14th October. As is common in India’s larger gig economy, individuals may be registered with several platforms at the same time. On the day of the incident, the individual had used Rapido’s services as a customer". The statement further read, “We are in constant touch with the authorities and are supporting them in their investigation. We responded promptly and have shared all the information requested from us. Rapido has zero tolerance for violence or criminal activity, and we will continue to extend our full cooperation.” - ABOUT THE AUTHOR Shashank Rao Shashank Rao is a Senior Assistant Editor having worked for over two decades. Fresh details have emerged in the shooting case involving Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff, with CCTV footage from Surat railway station helping police track down the three alleged assailants, who were arrested in Rajasthan’s Kota on Monday.

Shroff escaped unhurt after three motorcycle-borne assailants opened fire at him in Mumbai on Sunday evening as he was leaving a club in his car after playing football. The suspects subsequently travelled by road from Mumbai to Surat, where they boarded the Pune-Jaipur Express (train 12939). They were arrested in Kota on Monday morning while allegedly attempting to flee to Nepal via Delhi .
Also read: Shooters planned to kill Tiger Shroff in Mumbai, motive unclear, say police

According to railway officials, a team of Railway Police Force (RPF) and Government Railway Police (GRP) was formed based on inputs received from the police. "The surveillance footage was checked at various stations after which they were tracked from Surat railway station. The team of rail police along with local police apprehended them at Kota the next day, at around 10.15 am," said a Western Railway official.

news.headline: CJP's Abhijeet Dipke targets PM Modi over extended custody of Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka
news.story_lead: CJP's Abhijeet Dipke targets PM Modi over extended custody of Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka "Ashu and Saurav’s first crime was waving the Tiranga at Jantar Mantar. Their second crime? Refusing to back down," Abhijeet Dipke said in a post on X.
news.full_article_text: CJP's Abhijeet Dipke targets PM Modi over extended custody of Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka "Ashu and Saurav’s first crime was waving the Tiranga at Jantar Mantar. Their second crime? Refusing to back down," Abhijeet Dipke said in a post on X. Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke on Monday said party co-convenors Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka remained undeterred despite spending five days in jail, claiming they walked into court with smiles on their faces and their spirits unbroken. Das and Ranka were sent to judicial remand for another two days after being produced before a newly appointed Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) at Mandir Marg police station, an official said. "Ashu and Saurav’s first crime was waving the Tiranga at Jantar Mantar. Their second crime? Refusing to back down. Even after five days in jail, they walked into court with smiles on their faces, their spirits unbroken," Dipke said in a post on X. Deep Dive The two were initially sent to five-day judicial custody on October 13 after allegedly climbing over a locked gate to enter Jantar Mantar, which had earlier been denotified as a designated protest site. Also Read | CJP leaders Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka’s judicial custody extended by two days; Delhi Police cite ‘peace, tranquillity’ concerns Dipke targets PM Modi over detention In a lengthy Instagram post, Dipke accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi of using the state machinery to intimidate young protesters and suppress dissent. He questioned the government's decision to keep 26-27-year-old Saurav Das and 30-year-old Ashutosh Ranka in custody for waving the Tricolour at Jantar Mantar. "The great Vishwaguru Narendra Modi must be feeling very strong keeping 26-27-year-old Saurabh Das in jail and keeping 30-year-old Ashutosh behind bars. This is what strength looks like? Hiding behind the police, hiding behind the courts—is this Narendra Modi's strength?" he said. Dipke alleged that the duo had been denied timely hearings, with proceedings repeatedly postponed. He accused Modi of projecting strength by keeping young protesters behind bars and deploying the police and security forces against those opposing his government. Describing the two leaders' conduct in court as an example of courage, Dipke said Das had walked in with a smile even after spending five days in jail and learning that his judicial custody had been extended. He recalled that Das had once told him he would not be able to endure even a day in jail, but had remained composed despite spending five days in custody. "Real strength is knowing that you are fighting a power much greater than yourself. It is knowing what the consequences could be and still refusing to remain silent," he said. Dipke also recounted speaking to Das's mother, saying she remained confident that her son would not break despite being in jail. He said the resolve shown by the families of both leaders reflected the courage that the government had failed to intimidate. He said the continued detention of the two leaders would inspire more young people to speak out rather than deter them from protesting. Along with other party workers, Das and Ranka had displayed the national flag at Jantar Mantar and raised slogans against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar before being detained and placed under preventive arrest. On Sunday, the Special Executive Magistrate hearing their bail matter claimed that unknown persons were threatening him, following which police registered a non-cognisable report. In a post on X, Dipke alleged that the authorities were using delays to prolong the duo's detention. "The state is deliberately prolonging Ashu and Saurav's illegal arrest by using every dirty trick in the book to delay court proceedings and prevent their release. "They have no legal grounds to keep them behind bars, so they are resorting to delaying tactics to keep them there." The CJP also alleged that bail sureties submitted for the release of its leaders had been rejected on "vague" grounds. "Consequently, the Central District has put comprehensive arrangements in place, with police personnel, both male and female, deployed around the clock. Senior officers also conduct regular visits to the deployment sites. In light of this, we have ensured the deployment of an adequate police force," he added. The deployment will also focus on preventing pickpocketing, snatching and other street crimes that tend to pose a challenge in crowded areas during major festivals. Police teams will remain alert to any suspicious activity, officers said. Crowd management and traffic regulation will be key components of the security plan, particularly around major religious sites and venues hosting Dussehra events. Police personnel will coordinate with other agencies to ensure the smooth movement of devotees and visitors. Senior officers will monitor the arrangements and assess requirements at different locations, with additional personnel to be deployed wherever necessary, they said. Police have urged people to remain vigilant, follow instructions issued by security personnel and immediately report any suspicious object or activity to the nearest police officer. In Gurugram, police additional police personnel have been deployed at major venues, keeping in mind the size of the expected crowd. Police have identified 12 major and 54 small Ravan Dahan venues. Sixteen sites fall under the East Zone, 23 under the West Zone, seven under the South Zone and 20 under the Manesar Zone. The responsibilities of designated police officers and personnel have been clearly assigned at each site to ensure effective crowd control, security monitoring and maintenance of law and order. Special security arrangements have also been made for religious processions to be taken out across the district during Dussehra. Police personnel have been deployed for three processions in the East Zone, nine in the West Zone, two in the South Zone and three in the Manesar Zone, they added. One fire tender, one ambulance and one duty magistrate will be deployed at each of the 12 major Ravan Dahan sites. In addition, two fire tenders and two ambulances will remain on standby in each police zone to provide immediate assistance in case of an emergency, police said. In view of the anticipated increase in traffic around event venues during Dussehra, the traffic police will implement special traffic management measures. A separate, detailed duty roster has been issued for traffic and parking management, with dedicated personnel deployed accordingly, they added. "Special arrangements have been made to ensure public safety, facilitate smooth crowd management, maintain traffic discipline and respond effectively to any emergency situation with additional security arrangements. "In addition, one Quick Response Team (QRT) has been arranged for each police zone. To strengthen security at Dussehra fairs and other public events, special attention will be given to surveillance, public address systems, security checks and emergency response measures," A Gurugram Police spokesperson said. In Faridabad, special surveillance will be maintained at event venues, markets, major thoroughfares, and crowded areas. All concerned officers and Station House Officers (SHOs) have been directed to monitor security arrangements in their respective areas and maintain coordination with the organising committees, a Faridabad Police spokesperson said.

news.headline: British tourist sexually harassed in Kerala's Varkala, dress torn, video helps police arrest man
news.story_lead: British tourist sexually harassed in Kerala's Varkala, dress torn, video helps police arrest man The accused is expected to be produced before a court on Tuesday for remand. Further investigation is underway, police said. A British woman tourist was allegedly sexually harassed and had her dress torn by a man while returning to her room in Kerala’s Varkala around 1.30 am on Monday, police said.
news.full_article_text: British tourist sexually harassed in Kerala's Varkala, dress torn, video helps police arrest man The accused is expected to be produced before a court on Tuesday for remand. Further investigation is underway, police said. A British woman tourist was allegedly sexually harassed and had her dress torn by a man while returning to her room in Kerala’s Varkala around 1.30 am on Monday, police said. The accused, identified as Shahad, a resident of Odayam in Varkala, allegedly approached the woman as she was returning to her room after going out for food, and misbehaved with her before tearing her dress, police said, news agency PTI reported. The woman took refuge with a group of tourists, who intervened and stopped the accused. She approached the police on Monday morning, following which a case was registered. Police identified and arrested Shahad with the help of a video recorded by the woman. Meanwhile, in a separate case, a solo traveller currently hitchhiking across India shared an Instagram update about how her initial fears were dispelled by the kindness she encountered during her travels. Despite being warned about safety risks before arriving, the 24-year-old Portuguese creator, Ana, said that she experienced overwhelming helpfulness from people everywhere she went. “Before landing in India, everyone warned me about harassment, robbery, and stares. I was genuinely a bit afraid of going there and completely avoided hitchhiking for my entire first month in the country,” Ana wrote on Instagram. “But as time went by, the reality turned out to be completely different: Everywhere I went, I kept meeting the kindest, funniest, and most helpful people. From strangers on the street randomly spending two hours helping me fix a phone issue, to making lifelong friends—the men I met completely changed my perspective,” she added. - ABOUT THE AUTHOR Karishma Ayaldasani Karishma Ayaldasani is a Senior Content Producer at Hindustan Times, based in New Delhi, where she works with the digital team on fast-moving breaking stories from India and around the world. She enjoys covering national and global news, focusing on delivering updates quickly and clearly so readers can make sense of what’s happening as it unfolds. Comfortable in high-pressure newsroom settings, she regularly contributes to live blogs, explainers and real-time coverage. Before joining Hindustan Times, she was part of the digital team at The Indian Express, worked with the social media team at Firstpost, and spent time as a creative strategist at Clematis Advertising. Outside of work, she likes exploring different art forms and unwinds with music. It also said the two CJP leaders were granted police permission to protest ‘on the basis of their assurance that they would strictly adhere to the terms of permission’. However, they failed to adhere to the terms, it said. Flagging that the two had shown no ‘respect for law’, the order said, “At this stage, the grounds of apprehension as presented before me apparently suggests that the conduct of the respondents is not above board; rather it shows no respect for law and their habitualness in calling protest at de-notified areas.” It also said the the CJP leaders' statements that they will not repeat the ‘offence’ in future ‘does not inspire confidence’ as it cited the police investigation in the Jantar Mantar trespassing case. “The application filed by IO is supported by substantial material on record, raising serious concerns regarding the likelihood of breach of peace and disturbance of public tranquility, which cannot be brushed aside without proper consideration,” it said. A spokesman for the Saudi-backed Yemeni armed forces said the Iran-backed group launched three ballistic missiles at al-Alam camp near Ataq city, which was being used as a training centre for recruits to the security forces and police. The head of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, condemned what he called the "criminal attack" and promised a "firm response".

However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib and al-Jawf provinces. Shabwa province's media office said in a statement that ballistic missiles struck the Martyr Ahmed al-Sulaimani Training Centre, where recruits from several provinces were undergoing training to be members of the internal security forces. According to a preliminary assessment, 53 were killed and more than 200 injured, it added. A video posted on social media appeared to show several bodies scattered across the ground. Shabwa's deputy governor, Fahad al-Khalifi, told AFP news agency that hospitals in the province were overwhelmed and had been forced to transfer the most seriously wounded to neighbouring Hadramout and Aden, where the government is based. Some of them were in a critical condition, he said. Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said the attack constituted a war crime because the internal security forces training centre was not a military target. He also accused the Houthis of "attempting to fabricate a false media victory, boost the morale of its collapsing elements, and cover up the defeats and setbacks it is suffering across various combat axes". The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said in a statement that the missiles targeted a gathering of "Saudi enemy" forces at al-Alam camp, which he said was run by Saudi officers. There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities. In a separate development, Houthi-run media reported that a Saudi air strike on a home in the Sahar district of the Houthi-controlled northern province of Saada on Sunday killed at least 10 people and injured 23 others, many of them women and children. According to the Houthi-run health ministry in north-western Yemen, a total of 141 people had been killed in Saudi strikes over the past seven weeks. The government's health ministry, meanwhile, said last week that at least 1,282 people had been killed in the conflict across Yemen since 6 August. In Saudi Arabia, at least 19 people have been killed in Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom's airports since the beginning of October. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. Related topics
